ket_qua.statement: According to LKAB's company history, in 1736 a Sámi man named Amund Amundson Mangi reported the iron ore deposits in the Kiruna area to the Swedish state, and was rewarded with money and exemption from taxes for life.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: LKAB's own history attributes the 1736 report to Sámi man Amund Amundson Mangi and specifies a reward of 100 riksdaler and lifelong exemption from taxes, while acknowledging uncertainty in the historical record.

ket_qua.statement: Kiruna counts 1900 as its founding year, the year the King approved its town plan.

ket_qua.statement: LKAB's Kiruna mine carries out its production blasting every night between 01:15 and 01:45; the blasting area is evacuated beforehand, the mine is ventilated for a few hours afterwards, and vibrations can sometimes be felt above ground.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: LKAB confirms the 01:15–01:45 nightly production blasting window in Kiruna, prior evacuation, several hours of ventilation afterwards and occasional surface vibrations.

ket_qua.statement: LKAB, the Swedish state-owned mining company that operates the Kiruna mine, describes it as the world's largest underground iron ore mine (a description from LKAB itself, not independently confirmed).
ket_qua.ghi_chu: LKAB explicitly describes its Kiruna operation as the world's largest underground iron ore mine; this verdict verifies the company's attribution, not independent confirmation of the superlative.

ket_qua.statement: The current main haulage level of LKAB's Kiruna mine is at a depth of 1,365 metres (about 4,480 feet).
ket_qua.ghi_chu: LKAB identifies 1,365 metres as the current main haulage level in Kiruna, and its November 2026 announcement reconfirms this depth.

ket_qua.statement: LKAB mines Kiruna by sublevel caving: ore is extracted level by level from below and the overlying rock caves in behind the mining, so the ground surface above gradually subsides.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: LKAB explicitly identifies sublevel caving as its underground mining method and explains that the hanging-wall rock progressively fragments and caves into mined-out areas, causing mining-induced surface subsidence.

ket_qua.statement: The Kiruna ore body continues eastward beneath the old town (and northward), so ground deformation from mining continues to spread toward the town.

ket_qua.ghi_chu: LKAB explicitly confirmed both directions of ore-body extension in its August 2025 update and reported an expanded deformation forecast affecting additional homes and residents.

ket_qua.statement: On 18 May 2020 a magnitude 4.1 (ML, Swedish National Seismic Network) seismic event occurred at LKAB's Kiruna mine, the largest mining-induced earthquake recorded in Sweden; no one among the people in the mine was injured.
ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: 18 May 2020; magnitude ML 4.1; largest mining-induced earthquake in Scandinavia; 13 underground workers evacuated without injuries.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: A 2024 peer-reviewed study confirms ML 4.1 and identifies the event as Scandinavia's largest mining-induced earthquake; LKAB confirms that 13 workers escaped unharmed, although its operational measurements reported ML 3.3 and Mw 4.2.

ket_qua.statement: Iron ore trains on the Malmbanan line between Kiruna and Narvik run with up to 68 wagons and are about 750 m long, roughly the length of seven 105-metre football pitches.

ket_qua.ghi_chu: The Swedish Transport Administration confirms that Malmbanan accommodates trains up to 750 metres long with 68 wagons, and specifically reports approximately 12 loaded ore trains daily from Kiruna toward Narvik; the seven-football-pitch comparison is mathematically reasonable using 105-metre pitches.

ket_qua.statement: The sea off Luleå, Sweden's ore port on the northern Gulf of Bothnia east of Kiruna, freezes over every winter.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Visit Luleå explicitly states that the sea freezes every year because of the Gulf of Bothnia's relatively low salinity, although ice coverage and timing vary with winter conditions.

ket_qua.statement: The ore railway from Kiruna was built west over the mountains to the port of Narvik on the Norwegian coast, which LKAB says stays ice-free all year thanks to the warm Gulf Stream.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: LKAB confirms that the Iron Ore Line connects Kiruna with Narvik on the Norwegian coast and explicitly attributes Narvik's year-round ice-free port to the Gulf Stream.

ket_qua.statement: The railway reached Kiruna around 1900, the line to Narvik was completed in 1902, and it was officially inaugurated by King Oscar II in 1903.

ket_qua.statement: According to Trafikverket, about 12 loaded ore trains a day run from Kiruna to Narvik; Luleå remains an LKAB ore port, and winter shipping there relies on icebreaker assistance.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Trafikverket confirms approximately 12 loaded ore trains daily from Kiruna to Narvik; LKAB confirms Luleå remains an ore-export port, and official port and maritime sources confirm winter icebreaker assistance.

ket_qua.statement: Kiruna considers 1900 its year of birth, when the King approved the town plan.
